# Abstract

The board game market has grown rapidly, yet the quality of newly released games is hard to judge before player ratings accumulate. We confront this **cold-start problem** using data from BoardGameGeek (BGG): a complete pipeline collects 2,077 base games via BGG's offcial XML API2, and predicts two complementary quantities--*popularity* (regression, $R^2 \approx 0.73$) and *quality* (binary classification, test AUC up to 0.856) -- from a deliberately rating-free feature set of 10 structured attributes plus 30 latent text components from game description text themes as the strongest quality signal (71% of Gini importance; shuffling the text block drops test AUC by 0.078), and reveal that description length is a redundant proxy. After tuning the decision threshold on the precision–recall curve, we get an F1 of 0.71, compared with a 69.2% majority-class baseline. This is comparable to a leakage-prone variant that used popularity as a feature. We then turn the predictions into an interpretable content-based gamer recommender/finder and an interactive Streamlit app.

**Keywords:** cold-start problem, recommender systems, text mining, board games, interpretability.
